articleTitle: AI doomsday fears: what can ordinary people actually do?

sources.title: Your AI doomsday questions answered: ‘Why aren’t these companies being held to account?’
Your AI doomsday questions answered: ‘What, if anything, can people like me do about it?’

claims.claim: The Guardian and other outlets have hosted debates in which tech reporters Aisha Down, Blake Montgomery and Dan Milmo answer readers’ questions about the reality of an AI‑driven doomsday.

claims.claim: The reporters note that many of the scenarios—nuclear war, societal collapse or bioweapons—sound “too wooly to really take seriously.” They point out that the challenges of creating new deadly viruses are largely administrative, not technical, and that historical attempts such as Aum Shinrikyo’s botulism and anthrax spray have failed.
claims.bestSource: Your AI doomsday questions answered: ‘What, if anything, can people like me do about it?’
claims.evidence: Consider the failure of Aum Shinrikyo to kill vast numbers of people with botulism and anthrax by spraying these around central Tokyo. To be honest all sounds too wooly to really take seriously. Pottys99 Aisha: For what it’s worth, it seems unlikely that AI at this point can significantly change the equation around bioweapons or viruses … What has prevented bioweapon attacks through the past decades is not the difficulty of inventing new deadly viruses, but other, more prosaic issues.
claims.bestPassage: Consider the failure of Aum Shinrikyo to kill vast numbers of people with botulism and anthrax by spraying these around central Tokyo.

claims.claim: One researcher, Jacy Reese Anthis, has highlighted the “staggering gulf between how biological brains evolved and how AI systems are built.”
claims.bestSource: Your AI doomsday questions answered: ‘What, if anything, can people like me do about it?’
claims.evidence: Responding to Dawkins in the Guardian last year, Jacy Reese Anthis , a researcher in human AI interaction, said there was a “staggering gulf between how biological brains evolved and how AI systems are built”.

claims.claim: Critics of the AI industry say that the focus on a potential apocalypse distracts from elements of AI that are already inflicting widespread harm like algorithmic discrimination in housing allotment.

claims.claim: They also note that tech reporters feel a responsibility to question the power of “tech bros” and the concentration of wealth, but they admit that “there is, unfortunately, not much that comes to mind” for individuals to influence these issues.

editorial.claim: The Guardian interview highlights a perception that tech CEOs are shocked when the public’s opinion is negative.
Readers interested in the debate can follow updates from the tech reporters and keep an eye on policy proposals that aim to balance innovation with safety.
